title: Google Cloud launches Gemini for healthcare.
text:
Google Cloud launches Gemini for healthcare.
Google Cloud has announced Gemini for healthcare , an AI solution engineered to unify fragmented clinical, operational, and administrative systems. Moving beyond simple information retrieval, it enables healthcare teams to turn siloed data into coordinated action.
Clinicians lose nearly 28 hours each week to paperwork and administrative tasks, fueling burnout and straining budgets. By integrating specialized skills and data connectors with existing third-party systems, the platform brings together critical information from electronic health records, billing platforms, clinical guidelines, and Medicare datasets.
Gemini for healthcare reasons across this context to orchestrate and execute complex, multi-step workflows — such as medical records synthesis and prior authorization review — within defined guardrails and with appropriate human oversight. Initially available in preview alongside launch partners including HCA Healthcare, Highmark Health, and Northwell Health, it resolves bottlenecks and reclaims valuable staff time for patient care. Learn more on the Cloud blog .

title: Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
text:
Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace .
Why pay through Google Cloud?
Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs , deploying models with Inference Endpoints , calling thousands of models through Inference Providers , or hosting demos on GPU Spaces .
If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:
One bill : your Hugging Face usage appears on your existing Google Cloud invoice, next to the rest of your cloud spend.
No new vendor to onboard : purchases go through your existing Google Cloud billing account and procurement process.
Everything is covered : upgrading your org to a Team or Enterprise subscription, pay-as-you-go compute (Jobs, Inference Endpoints, Inference Providers, GPU Spaces, ZeroGPU quota extension), and additional storage at public Hugging Face pricing .
If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.
1. Subscribe to Hugging Face on the Google Cloud Marketplace
Go to the Hugging Face Hub listing on the Google Cloud Marketplace, select the Google Cloud project you want to use, and click on "Subscribe".
You are now on the subscription page. Select the billing account to be charged, review and accept the terms, then click "Subscribe".
Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.
2. Link your Hugging Face organization
You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.
You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.
Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.
3. Subscription approved
Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.
To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization : the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.
Congratulations!
Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.
A few things worth knowing:
Google Cloud replaces the credit card as the organization's payment method. Usage is metered and reported to Google Cloud, so adding credits is not available while the organization is billed through the marketplace.
Included credits still apply : if your organization has a Team or Enterprise subscription, the monthly included credits are applied before any pay-as-you-go usage is reported to Google Cloud.
Monitor your usage at any time from the billing section of your organization settings , and find the charges in the Billing reports of the Google Cloud console.
Linking and unlinking are audited : both actions are recorded in your organization's audit logs .
Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation . If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co .

title: Decision Models in Hugging Face
text:
Decision Models in Hugging Face
Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.
Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:
"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."
The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.
We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.
But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ?
This is the key idea behind decision models .
What are decision models?
A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.
TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).
The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models )
For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:
Why not use LLMs for everything?
We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.
However, there are a few problems with this approach.
LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices.
Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work.
Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.
How are decision models different from classification models?
Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.
Traditional classification
Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:
A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.
The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head .
If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.
Zero-shot classification
Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.
Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.
One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.
This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.
Where decision models differ
Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).
More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions .
Consider these three approaches:
Probability over choices
Yes
Labels defined at inference
No
Multiple typed questions
Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions

Possible with adaptation
Native primitives
The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.
The decision model interface
A decision model request has the following two components:
State
The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.
Questions and their primitives
Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:
Choice: Select one of several possible answers.
Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale.
Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically.
Let's go over them one by one.
Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.
Which department should handle this customer request?
The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.
The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion
text:
Anthropic intends to push ahead with its IPO despite shakier markets and the broader pullback from AI investing.
The Claude-maker said in an updated IPO filing on Tuesday that it would be offering a total of 825 million Class A shares at an estimated price range of $70 to $78 per share. The sale is expected to raise anywhere from $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion.
The company could end up being worth a hefty $1.404 trillion if its shares list at the top of the price range, on a fully diluted basis. That would represent a significant jump up from the $965 billion valuation Anthropic reached in a May fundraise , but it’s still lower than the $2 trillion the company was reportedly targeting a couple months ago.
Separately, Anthropic said it had struck a deal to privately sell $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC. Google and Nvidia are investing $10 billion apiece.
All up, Anthropic estimates net proceeds to reach somewhere between $84.6 billion and $93.7 billion (the latter if the IPO underwriters exercise their option to buy additional shares).
Underwriters, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, will have the option to buy up to 123.75 million more shares from Anthropic at the IPO price.
As a public benefit corporation, the founders hold a Class F share with 50.1% of the voting power. The Long-Term Benefit Trust will also elect a board majority, so Class A buyers will have limited influence.
Anthropic intends to start trading on the Nasdaq close to November 19, per reporting from CNBC , under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The company expects up to 20% of the offering to be allocated to retail investors.
Anthropic also gave out a few new details in the updated filing. The company said its run-rate revenue reached $81 billion by the end of October, about $10 billion more than at the end of September.
Also, the filing now lists how many shares the company’s co-founders expect to sell in the IPO: CEO Dario Amodei, president and chairperson Daniela Amodei, chief compute officer Tom Brown, Anthropic Institute head Jack Clark, chief science officer Jared Kaplan, chief architect Sam McCandlish, and interpretability research lead Christopher Olah are all selling nearly 3.4 million shares each. At the $74 midpoint of the IPO price range, that would land them about $250 million each.
The updated filing also has a small but important change that hints at the company’s stance toward the Trump administration: The company at many points uses “super intelligence” and “SI” interchangeably with “artificial intelligence” and “AI,” citing Trump’s executive order from September that directed government departments and agencies to use that new terminology to refer to AI.
The company’s third-quarter revenue came in at $17 billion, and nine-month revenue was $33.2 billion. The company reported a nine-month net loss of $104 billion, with compute and infrastructure commitments hitting $900.9 billion. It has nearly $132 billion in cash and short-term investments.
OpenAI, Anthropic’s biggest rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after it raised $11 billion, nearly half the $20 billion it had first tried to raise.

title: Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion IPO
text:
Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion IPO
Anthropic’s public offering is expected to make it one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies as soon as next week.
Anthropic confirmed on Tuesday that its IPO could be one of the biggest ever, even while falling short of previous expectations. Its IPO price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share, which would put its valuation as high as $1.4 trillion, according to the The New York Times . The Wall Street Journal reports that according to its sources, Anthropic is “aiming for its shares to start trading Thursday or Friday next week.”
As Reuters notes, the Anthropic IPO was previously expected to be valued at as much as $2 trillion. As of last week, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion .
Those lower expectations follow months of debate around AI safety , and what that means, while midterm election results showed souring public opinion toward AI companies and data center projects they’re heavily investing in. And that doesn’t even include this past weekend’s revelations about an alleged Chinese spy’s involvement with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang .
The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”

title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
text:
The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested.
As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket.
Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI.
“With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”
Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute.
Related
What could China get from Jensen Huang?
The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life?
Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged.
Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI.
Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge . “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”
It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China.
Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says.
Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions.
Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge . “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.”
The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says.
Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan.
“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.”
But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke.
“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says.
Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. If those distractions begin to affect Nvidia’s ability to execute — slowing decisions, product rollouts, or the allocation of already scarce chips — the consequences could quickly reach customers. title: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
text:
No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang . He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US–China relations. That now all stands in the balance.
Over the past few days, Huang’s status as an AI titan has come under scrutiny amid an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang , an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia’s board of directors said the company would launch an investigation into the incident. Huang, the company said, “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” Huang earned $36 million last year and owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March, according to a corporate filing—which also noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go anytime without severance.
How exactly the investigation shakes out, and what it means for Huang’s future at the company, remains to be seen. But the incident at least puts his position at risk, and raises questions about how the industry will respond.
“He’s the person who decides who gets the chips and who doesn't,” says David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who tracks the chip industry.
Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models. With those chips in short supply, Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost next. Nvidia has also bankrolled much of the AI buildout, investing billions in the very companies buying its chips, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. When Elon Musk wants to build a new data center, Yoffie says, he can put in a call to Huang.
Internally, Huang closely manages even small details at Nvidia, responds to emails from any one of its roughly 60,000 staffers, and raises his voice to get points across, according to current and former employees. He’s a regular on cable TV and at tech conferences, where he’s been trying to deflate concerns about an AI market bubble and boost the positioning of his company .
But Nvidia has no other executive anywhere close to Huang’s prominence, and no apparent potential successor. “We have no idea who would replace him,” Yoffie says. “You put someone new into that position, if you're a customer, who knows what that's going to mean.”
Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, says Huang has played such an important role—and become so close to the president—that he has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry.
“On the one hand, Huang is irreplaceable. He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution,” Fedasiuk says. But he says that the company, which is indispensable to the AI industry, has to come first.
“He has to be replaceable as the CEO of the world's largest company, at $4 trillion in capex.”
Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose.
The board’s investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies, Yoffie says. But the FBI could also investigate whether laws were broken, and Congress may decide to look into whether Huang’s affair influenced the US government’s policy on selling chips to China.
Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The scandal also raises serious questions about whether China may have gained sensitive information about US AI companies and the government’s strategy on China, Fedasiuk says.
Huang’s affair appears especially damning given how outspoken he has been in recent years against calls for more aggressive technology export controls on China. His credibility on the topic could be permanently in doubt.
Both the first Trump administration and the Biden administration imposed export controls designed to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, as well as to technology required to mint advanced semiconductors. In his second term, however, Trump loosened these controls, giving China access to older generations of Nvidia chips; it was better to make China reliant on US technology, the argument went.
Sam Bresnick , a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, says the Huang scandal is likely to accelerate efforts to crack down on chip exports.
“There was going to be more of an impetus to control what chips are getting sent to China anyway,” he says. “I expect there to be more scrutiny on what's going on, what's getting sent to China. I think there's also going to be more scrutiny from the Commerce Department.”

title: All 7 Anthropic founders will each cash out about $250M in IPO
text:
As Anthropic barrels toward an enormous IPO that could value it at $1.4 trillion, the company has disclosed a tidbit in its new S-1 filing about how many shares each of its seven co-founders plan to sell.
Each will sell 3,378,378 shares. Anthropic has floated an unusually broad initial price range of $70 to $78 a share. At the midrange of $74, each founder would take in just shy of $250 million.
At the low end, $70, each would have to settle for pocketing just over $236 million in cash; at the high end, $78, each would take in just under $264 million.
However, in an IPO as eagerly anticipated as this one, companies can often price shares above the initial range.
The S-1 is already hinting at high demand. Board member Reed Hastings has indicated he wants to buy $300 million worth of shares through his donor-advised fund. Board member Christopher Liddell also wants to buy $3 million worth of shares.
The seven co-founders are Dario Amodei, CEO; Daniela Amodei, president and chair of the board; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer (pictured above); Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Christopher Olah, interpretability research lead.
After the sale, each of them will own about 3.2% of the total outstanding Class A shares, the S-1 says, or roughly 22% collectively. That’s not their share of the company overall. Class A is just one of Anthropic’s share classes, and other holders, including Amazon and Google, hold nonvoting Class N shares, so the founders’ stake in the company’s total equity will be considerably smaller. Even still, they, as a group, remain in control of the company. Each will also receive one share of Class F stock, which carries supervoting rights. Collectively, the founders will control 51.1% of the votes, but no single founder will hold significantly more shares or votes than the others.
As is now industry lore, the seven left OpenAI to start Anthropic in 2021 after disagreements with OpenAI’s leadership over how AI should be built. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who held senior research and policy roles at OpenAI, were joined by five fellow OpenAI colleagues in forming a company that has said, very publicly and from the start, that it’s more focused on AI safety than its rivals, including the founders’ former employer.

title: We’re bringing Adobe’s creative and productivity tools closer to your everyday Google apps.
text:
We’re bringing Adobe’s creative and productivity tools closer to your everyday Google apps.
Today at Adobe MAX, we announced we’re expanding our partnership with Adobe.
Switching between apps to edit a PDF or fine-tune an image can quickly break your focus. Our partnership will bring Adobe’s creative and productivity tools directly into the Google products you use every day. It will also bring Google’s frontier AI models into Adobe’s apps. Here’s what’s coming:
Work faster with PDFs: You’ll soon have a direct pathway from Google Drive and Gmail into Adobe Acrobat, surfaced as a suggested app across both services, including an “Edit with” entry point in file previews.
Create right where you search and chat: Adobe is expanding its connectors in Gemini and Gemini Enterprise with Acrobat and additional creative tools. Adobe will also bring its creative tools to AI Mode in Google Search.
Powering creatives and enterprises: Businesses will be able to use Adobe’s CX Enterprise Coworker agent in Gemini Enterprise — an AI assistant that helps teams design graphics, work with PDFs, and launch marketing campaigns without switching apps.
Exploring editing experiences with DeepMind: Adobe and Google DeepMind will explore new editing capabilities for creative professionals, starting with an image model for Photoshop that could enable near-real-time edits.

title: Adobe brings AI agents and new creative tools to Photoshop, Premiere, and Firefly
text:
Adobe is pouring more AI into its products, including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, and InDesign, in a major product feature announcement at its MAX event in Miami. The company is also expanding AI capabilities in its creative tool, Firefly, and releasing a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that lets other chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini use Adobe features.
Adobe’s Firefly app is moving into Figma’s territory with a new prototyping tool in private beta called Builder, which lets users create designs to show off ideas. There is also a new tool to create on-brand graphs, along with an image-editing tool that lets you change part of an image without changing other objects.
A new AI-powered video tool in Firefly will allow users to assemble a video from clips and other elements like images and sound effects. The company is making its agent proactive and always on so that it can get more context about work and be present for any action. Adobe is also making it easier for people to take quick action, like removing the background or generating a thumbnail for a video.
The company has already added a ton of AI features across its apps like Photoshop, Express, Premiere, and Illustrator . At the MAX event, Adobe is continuing the trend. Photoshop is getting a new relighting feature and sliders for prompt-based generative styles; Premiere will have a new color grading system for professionals and an object removal feature for video; and Lightroom has a way to correct blinking eyes and a blemish removal tool.
Adobe already offers a lot of third-party models from companies like Google, Runway, ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs, OpenAI, Kling, and ByteDance. One of its newer acquisitions, Topaz Labs , is releasing two image models, called Wonder 4 for upscaling and denoising, and ImageHDR, to turn standard images into HDR.
The company already has ChatGPT and Claude integrations to let users access some of its product functions. Now, Adobe is releasing a local MCP to expose more features of its Creative Cloud apps to users.
Adobe vice president Deepa Subramaniam told TechCrunch that the company is still figuring out what capabilities to expose and will rely on user feedback.
“We are still figuring out where and when and how to draw the line. What we’re putting out there is a number of endpoints and capabilities across Illustrator, Photoshop, After Effects, and Premiere. We’re just going to see how people use it, what they’re trying to do, and keep showing more. We don’t have any need or desire to sort of limit what the MCP endpoint can expose. What we really want to do is to support that creative workflow, how you choose to do it,” said Subramaniam.
Last month, Adobe rival Figma co-founder Dylan Field said at an event in India that MCP is not a perfect standard and benefits frontier labs more .
